# How does the index look like?

Day 2, 16:15 · Google · coverage: transcript

The speaker refers back to the earlier talk on tokenization (Understanding what's on a page). No slides were photographed.

## Claims

- **[Stage]** The speaker recapped Google's pipeline up to the index: Google crawls pages, processes the fetched documents and then stores them in its index.
  <br><sub>`D2-C719` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works) · Repeats [D1-C036](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's Search index stores the tokens produced by tokenizing each page, as they are, together with the metadata attached to the tokens during tokenization.
  <br><sub>`D2-C720` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · not in Google docs · Repeats [D2-C323](../day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) · Used by `DEV-HTM-07`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's Search index does not hold the full content of pages; Google said storing full pages and pulling them out at serving time would be a very inefficient way of doing search.
  > "we don't have the full content of the page in our index"
  <br><sub>`D2-C721` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · not in Google docs · Repeats [D2-C318](../day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Each document in Google's index has pretty much all the signals calculated for it attached, for example quality signals plus the page's country and language, according to an illustration the speaker called an approximation of the real structure.
  <br><sub>`D2-C722` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works) · Extends [D1-C037](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Repeated by [D3-C076](../day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) · Extended by [D3-C079](../day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) · Extended by [D3-C083](../day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** The snippet shown for a web result is reconstructed from the tokens stored in Google's index: Google knows the position of each token in the document and rebuilds the snippet from those positions.
  > "the snippet that you see was reconstructed from these tokens"
  <br><sub>`D2-C724` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D3-C316](../day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's snippet documentation says snippets are created automatically, primarily from the page content, to preview the part that best relates to the user's specific search, so one page can get different snippets for different searches; sometimes the meta description is used instead.
  <br><sub>`D2-C725` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, How does the index look like? · is the documentation · [Control your snippets in search results](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/snippet) · Used by `DEV-HTM-03`</sub>

- **[Stage]** AI Overviews and AI Mode use the same index structures and token-based snippets as classic web results, a point Google called important but not obvious.
  <br><sub>`D2-C726` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide), [AI features and your website](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features), [Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag) · Extends [D1-C038](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Extended by [D3-C325](../day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) · Repeated by [D3-C702](../day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said that when AI Overviews or AI Mode run a query fan-out, the generated queries are sent to Google's Search index and documents come back with their snippets, which then feed the AI-generated answer (part of this passage is unclear in the recording).
  <br><sub>`D2-C727` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide), [AI features and your website](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features), [Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag) · Extends [D1-C053](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Extends [D1-C051](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Extends [D2-C073](../day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) · Extends [D1-C172](../day1/D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md) · Extended by [D3-C059](../day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's robots meta tag specification says the nosnippet rule also prevents a page's content from being used as a direct input for AI Overviews and AI Mode, and max-snippet also limits how much of it may be used that way.
  <br><sub>`D2-C728` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, How does the index look like? · is the documentation · [Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag) · Used by `DEV-IDX-05`, the glossary term *max-snippet*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google says query fan-out in AI Overviews and AI Mode issues related searches across subtopics and several data sources, which for AI Mode include the Knowledge Graph and shopping data as well as web content (AI Mode launch post, March 2025).
  <br><sub>`D2-C729` · Google Search Central, Google blog (5 March 2025) · annotates Day 2, How does the index look like? · is the documentation · [AI features and your website](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features), [Expanding AI Overviews and introducing AI Mode](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/search/ai-mode-search/) · Extends [D1-C053](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Extended by [D3-C061](../day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) · Used by the glossary term *Query fan-out*</sub>

- **[Analysis]** There is no separate AI index to optimise for: when a page never shows up as a source in AI Overviews or AI Mode, first check that it is indexed, that no nosnippet rule blocks its snippet and that the site is not excluded in Search Console's generative AI setting, the eligibility conditions Google lists.
  <br><sub>`D2-C730` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, How does the index look like? · [AI features and your website](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features), [Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide) · Used by `DEV-AIF-01`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Treat nosnippet, data-nosnippet and max-snippet as AI visibility settings too: Google lists them as the controls for content in AI features, and if AI answers are built from index snippets, as Google said on stage, a blocked or shortened snippet leaves AI Overviews and AI Mode less to use.
  <br><sub>`D2-C731` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, How does the index look like? · [AI features and your website](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features), [Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag)</sub>

- **[Stage]** To find relevant pages, Google's serving system relies on posting lists, a long-established information retrieval structure taught in computer science courses, because simply asking for every page that contains a word would not work.
  <br><sub>`D2-C732` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [How Google Search organizes information](https://www.google.com/search/howsearchworks/how-search-works/organizing-information/) · Extended by [D2-C824](../day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) · Used by the glossary term *Posting list*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said posting lists, which Google's serving system uses to find the pages that contain a query's words, are not new: they are at least 60 years old (as of 2026).
  <br><sub>`D2-C824` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C732](../day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** For most of the tokens Google finds on the web, though not every single one, the index keeps a posting list of the URLs that contain that token.
  <br><sub>`D2-C733` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · not in Google docs · Repeated by [D3-C074](../day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) · Used by the glossary term *Posting list*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's How Search Works site describes the Search index as like the index at the back of a book, with an entry for every word seen on every webpage Google indexes.
  > "It’s like the index in the back of a book - with an entry for every word seen on every webpage we index."
  <br><sub>`D2-C734` · Google Search (How Search Works) · annotates Day 2, How does the index look like? · is the documentation · [How Google Search organizes information](https://www.google.com/search/howsearchworks/how-search-works/organizing-information/)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The speaker's 'most of the tokens' is more precise than the public explainer's 'an entry for every word': the explainer simplifies, and the speaker's self-correction suggests some tokens get no posting list, though the speaker did not say which.
  <br><sub>`D2-C735` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, How does the index look like?</sub>

- **[Stage]** In posting-list retrieval, the posting lists of the query's words are intersected, which yields an unranked list of candidate URLs.
  <br><sub>`D2-C736` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D3-C075](../day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) · Used by the glossary term *Posting list*</sub>

- **[Stage]** A search query is broken into words with the same segmenter or tokenizer that Google used to build the index.
  <br><sub>`D2-C737` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · not in Google docs · Repeats [D2-C321](../day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) · Extended by [D3-C013](../day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** At retrieval, Google looks up the posting lists of the query words that are actually important rather than of every word in the query.
  <br><sub>`D2-C738` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D3-C075](../day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Besides posting lists, Google can retrieve documents through vector embeddings: parts of documents are associated with embeddings, which form a vector space used for retrieval.
  > "just like you build a posting list, you can also build a vector space"
  <br><sub>`D2-C740` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [How AI powers great search results](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/search/how-ai-powers-great-search-results/), [A guide to Google Search ranking systems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ranking-systems-guide) · Extended by [D3-C077](../day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) · Extended by [D3-C311](../day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) · Used by the glossary term *Vector embeddings*</sub>

- **[Stage]** In embedding-based retrieval, the distance between the embeddings of documents and the embedding of the user's query decides which documents are returned.
  <br><sub>`D2-C741` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [How AI powers great search results](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/search/how-ai-powers-great-search-results/), [A guide to Google Search ranking systems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ranking-systems-guide) · Extends [D1-C129](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Used by the glossary term *Vector embeddings*</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Write for both retrieval routes without keyword stuffing: name the page's subject in the plain words people search with, because posting lists match the words on the page, and explain the topic fully, because embedding retrieval matches meaning, so every keyword variation is unnecessary.
  <br><sub>`D2-C742` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, How does the index look like? · [Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/seo-starter-guide), [Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said a vector space also holds embeddings for associations the web makes with a page, such as what is known about its author; most of them sit far from typical queries, and a query that names the association may move closer to them.
  <br><sub>`D2-C744` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Both retrieval methods Google described, the long-established posting lists and the newer vector embeddings, work from the content of the page.
  <br><sub>`D2-C745` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [How Google Search organizes information](https://www.google.com/search/howsearchworks/how-search-works/organizing-information/), [How AI powers great search results](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/search/how-ai-powers-great-search-results/)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said, hedging with 'I think', that because retrieval is still based on content, the content mantra Google started about 25 years ago (as of 2026) still stands.
  > "this mantra that we started 25 years ago or whatever still stands, whether we like it or not"
  <br><sub>`D2-C746` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google)</sub>
